title: Database Concepts & Relational Thinking
learning_objective: Describe how a relational database organises data into linked tables, identify the primary key and any foreign keys in a given schema, and explain when a database is preferable to a spreadsheet.
description_for_ai: A table holds one kind of thing, and its grain is what a single row represents (e.g. one row per customer). A primary key is the column, or set of columns, whose values are unique for every row and identify that row unambiguously (e.g. customer_id in a customers table); it should not be a column like full_name that merely looks unique. A foreign key is a column in one table that references a primary key in another table (e.g. orders.customer_id references customers.customer_id) and does not itself uniquely identify the row it appears in. Splitting data across linked tables avoids storing the same fact in many places: a customer's name is stored once in customers rather than repeated on every order row, so renaming them means updating one row, not many. A database enforces rules a spreadsheet cannot: uniqueness on a primary key, referential integrity on a foreign key (rejecting a value that does not exist in the referenced table), and safe simultaneous edits by multiple users. This makes a database the better tool once data is shared, growing, or must stay consistent across many people touching it; a spreadsheet remains fine for a quick, single-person, one-off list.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Nominating a column like full_name or email as a primary key because it looks unique, without recognising two different rows could share it. Assuming a foreign key column must share the exact same name as the primary key it references. Treating 'a database is always better' as a blanket rule rather than recognising each tool fits different situations. Confusing a table's grain (what one row represents) with its row count (how many rows exist).
not_yet_taught: star schema / fact and dimension tables

title: Core Querying: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY
learning_objective: Write a SELECT query that retrieves specific columns from a single table, filters rows with WHERE using comparison and logical operators, and sorts the result with ORDER BY, to answer a stated business question.
description_for_ai: SELECT names which columns to return; naming columns explicitly (SELECT full_name, city FROM customers) is the default in real work, with SELECT * reserved for quick exploration. FROM names the source table. WHERE filters rows using comparison operators (=, !=, >, <, >=, <=); text values must be wrapped in single quotes (WHERE city = 'Lagos') or SQLite reads the value as a column name rather than a string, causing an error. AND requires every condition to hold and can only return as many or fewer rows than OR on the same conditions, since OR requires only one condition to hold. ORDER BY sorts the result; ascending is the default and ASC can be omitted, while DESC must be stated explicitly to rank the highest or latest value first. Clause order is fixed: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, and this order cannot be rearranged.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Omitting single quotes around a text literal in WHERE, causing an error because the value is read as an identifier. Expecting AND to return more rows than OR on the same two conditions, when AND can only match as many or fewer. Writing WHERE after ORDER BY, which is a syntax error given the fixed clause order. Forgetting that leaving off DESC silently sorts ascending rather than descending.
example_code_for_ai:
SELECT full_name, city, total_spent
FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Lagos' AND membership_tier = 'Gold'
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
-- Returns Gold-tier Lagos customers, highest spender first
not_yet_taught: star schema / fact and dimension tables

title: Aggregation & Grouping
learning_objective: Use GROUP BY with aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) to summarise data by category, filter groups with HAVING, and verify a computed total against a known reference figure before trusting it.
description_for_ai: Aggregate functions collapse many rows into one summary value: COUNT(*) counts every row regardless of NULLs, COUNT(column) counts only the non-NULL values in that column, and SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX operate on a numeric column while ignoring NULLs. Without GROUP BY, an aggregate summarises the whole table into a single row. GROUP BY column splits the table into one bucket per distinct value first, then aggregates within each bucket, producing one summary row per group. Once GROUP BY is used, every column in SELECT must be either the grouped column itself or wrapped in an aggregate function, because a bare non-aggregated, non-grouped column has no single value to show per group. HAVING filters groups after aggregation and is the only clause that can test an aggregate condition (HAVING SUM(total_spent) > 100000); WHERE cannot, because it executes before grouping happens and the aggregate does not exist yet. A computed total should be checked against an independently known reference figure before being trusted, since a query returning a plausible number without an error is not proof that the number is correct.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Writing an aggregate condition in WHERE instead of HAVING, which errors because WHERE runs before the aggregate exists. Adding a non-aggregated, non-grouped column to SELECT alongside GROUP BY. Confusing COUNT(*) with COUNT(column) when the column contains NULLs, producing two different, both-plausible-looking counts. Trusting a total the moment the query runs without error, without checking it against any known reference number.
example_code_for_ai:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customer_count, SUM(total_spent) AS total_spend
FROM customers
GROUP BY city
HAVING SUM(total_spent) > 100000
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;
-- One row per city, keeping only cities whose combined spend exceeds 100000
not_yet_taught: star schema / fact and dimension tables

title: Joins & Subqueries
learning_objective: Combine two tables with INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN, predict the row count a join will return before running it, and use a subquery to answer a question that needs a list or value from one table before filtering another.
description_for_ai: A JOIN combines rows from two tables using an ON condition naming the shared key (FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id). INNER JOIN keeps only rows where the ON condition finds a match in both tables, so a customer with no matching order is dropped entirely. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left-hand table regardless of a match; unmatched rows receive NULL in every right-hand column, which is different from zero or an error. Before running a join, the row count should be predicted: an INNER JOIN's result has one row per matching child record (e.g. per order with a valid customer), and a LEFT JOIN's result adds one extra row for every left-hand row with zero matches. WHERE right_table.column IS NULL after a LEFT JOIN is the standard pattern for finding rows in the left table with no match in the right table. A subquery is a complete query nested inside another, usually in parentheses; a scalar subquery returns one value used in a comparison (WHERE total_spent > (SELECT AVG(total_spent) FROM customers)), and an IN subquery returns a list of values used to filter (WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'Delivered')).
common_mistakes_for_ai: Using INNER JOIN when the question requires unmatched rows to be kept, silently dropping the exact rows the question was asking about. Expecting a LEFT JOIN to return fewer rows than an INNER JOIN on the same tables, when it never returns fewer, only ever adds rows. Forgetting the subquery's own WHERE clause and pulling in unrelated rows as a result. Skipping the row-count prediction before running a join, so an inflated result from an unexpected duplicate key goes unnoticed.
example_code_for_ai:
SELECT c.full_name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
-- Customers with zero orders: LEFT JOIN keeps them, IS NULL isolates the unmatched rows
not_yet_taught: star schema / fact and dimension tables

title: Warehousing Fundamentals
learning_objective: Describe the difference between a transactional (OLTP) database and a data warehouse, and identify the fact table and dimension tables in a star schema.
description_for_ai: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) describes a database tuned for many small, fast, safe reads and writes supporting a live application, normalised into linked tables so a single row updates quickly without duplicating data. A data warehouse holds a separate, reshaped copy of the same underlying data, loaded on a schedule rather than updated instantly, optimised for a small number of heavy analytical queries (e.g. total revenue by category across two years) so those heavy queries never compete with the live application for resources. A star schema is the typical shape of a warehouse: one fact table at the centre, holding numeric measures (e.g. quantity, line_total) plus foreign keys out to every dimension, with its grain being one row per measurable event; several dimension tables surround it, each holding descriptive, mostly-text attributes (e.g. product name, category) with one clear primary key and few or no foreign keys of its own, growing far more slowly than the fact table. A fact table is identified by numeric columns meant to be summed plus several foreign keys and rapid row growth; a dimension table is identified by descriptive text columns meant to be grouped by, not summed, with a stable, slow-growing row count.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming a table is a fact table because of its name rather than examining its actual columns. Believing a warehouse is updated in real time the same way an OLTP database is. Treating OLTP and warehouse as better/worse rather than built for different jobs. Confusing a dimension table's own primary key with the fact table's foreign key that references it.
example_code_for_ai:
-- fact table: one row per sale, numeric measures, foreign keys out
CREATE TABLE fact_sales (
    sale_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    date_key TEXT,
    product_key TEXT,
    quantity INTEGER,
    line_total INTEGER
);

-- dimension table: descriptive, one row per product
CREATE TABLE dim_product (
    product_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    product_name TEXT,
    category TEXT
);

title: AI-Augmented SQL
learning_objective: Translate a business question into a natural-language prompt precise enough to produce a correct SQL query, critically read AI-written SQL for errors using a structured checklist, and verify a query's result against a prediction or known reference before trusting it.
description_for_ai: A precise prompt names the exact tables and columns involved, states the exact business logic (e.g. 'distinct customers' rather than just 'customers'), gives exact filter bounds (e.g. an inclusive date range with explicit start and end dates), and states the expected shape of the answer; a vague prompt leaves the AI to fill gaps with its own assumption, which may not match what was meant. AI-written SQL should be checked against five things before running it: whether the schema (tables and columns) actually exists and means what was assumed, whether clauses are in the fixed SELECT/FROM/WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING/ORDER BY order with WHERE used for row-level conditions and HAVING reserved for aggregate conditions, whether the join type matches whether unmatched rows should be kept, a predicted row count or value stated before running the query, and finally the actual result compared against that prediction or an independently known reference. A query running without any error is not proof it is correct. Common AI mistakes include COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(DISTINCT column) after a join, which silently inflates a count when one row on the left matches several rows on the right; INNER JOIN where LEFT JOIN was needed, silently dropping rows with no match; and an exclusive date bound where an inclusive one was intended.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Accepting an AI-written query as correct simply because it executed without an error message. Treating 'AI wrote it' as itself the reason a query is trustworthy. Regenerating the same vague prompt repeatedly, hoping for a different, correct-looking answer, instead of fixing the prompt or the query directly. Skipping the row-count or value prediction step because the query looks right at a glance.
example_code_for_ai:
-- Prompt left "unique" unstated; AI wrote this, which double-counts:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-31';

-- Corrected after predicting and checking the result:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c.customer_id) AS customer_count
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-31';
